lesson.title: Sketching the Trend: Finding a Line of Best Fit
lesson.summary: When scatterplot data trends in a clear direction, a single straight line, the line of best fit, can summarize that trend and let you write its equation.
lesson.body:
A scatterplot shows you paired data as points on the coordinate plane, and correlation tells you whether those points trend up, down, or not at all. When there is a clear positive or negative trend, it is often useful to describe that trend with a single straight line rather than just pointing at the general direction. That line is called the line of best fit, or trend line, a straight line drawn through the data that comes as close as possible to representing the overall pattern.

Why bother with a line at all? Two big reasons. First, a line gives you one equation, in the slope-intercept form y = mx + b you already know from graphing lines, that summarizes the whole relationship in a compact way. Second, that equation lets you make predictions: you can estimate a y-value for an x-value that is not even in your original data set, as long as it falls near the range you actually observed.

Here is the by-hand method for drawing a line of best fit. Plot every point first. Look at the cloud of points and imagine a straight line running through the middle of it, with roughly as many points above the line as below it, following the overall tilt of the data. The line does not need to pass through any specific data point, and usually will not pass through most of them. Once you have a line you are happy with, pick two points that lie on your line, they can be actual data points if those happen to sit on the line, or they can be points you read off the line itself, and use them to find the slope and equation, exactly as you would for any line.

Worked example. Five students record how many hours they studied for a quiz and the score they earned out of 10 points:

Hours studied: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Quiz score: 3, 5, 4, 8, 10

Plotting these points shows an overall upward trend, a positive correlation, even though the third point dips slightly, 3 hours only earned a 4, lower than the 5 earned after just 2 hours. A reasonable line of best fit can be drawn from around (1, 3) to around (5, 10), since those two points sit close to the overall direction of the cloud. The slope between them is m = (10 - 3) / (5 - 1) = 7/4 = 1.75. Using the point (1, 3) in point-slope form: y - 3 = 1.75(x - 1), which simplifies to y = 1.75x + 1.25.

This equation says each additional hour of studying is associated with roughly 1.75 more points on the quiz, and it predicts a score of about 1.25 for zero hours of studying, though that prediction reaches slightly outside the data you actually collected, so it is less trustworthy. Notice, too, that the line does not fit every point perfectly. At x = 3, the line predicts 1.75(3) + 1.25 = 6.5, but the actual score was only 4. That is expected, a line of best fit approximates the trend in the data, it is not required to touch every point.

One limitation of this by-eye method is that it depends on which two points you choose to draw through. Another student looking at the same scatterplot might sketch a slightly different line and get a slightly different equation, and there is no way to say for certain which by-eye line is truly the best one. That uncertainty is exactly the problem linear regression is built to solve.
